chunks: Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿUqbah, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

A man asked him, while I was with him, about a man who struck another man and caused his urination to be cut off. So he said to him: “If the urine does not pass until the night, then the full diyah is upon him, because he has prevented his livelihood. If it lasts until the end of the day, then the diyah is upon him. If it lasts until midday, then two-thirds of the diyah is upon him. And if it lasts until the day has risen high, then one-third of the diyah is upon him.”

key_terms.ارْتِفَاعِ النَّهَارِ: the rise of the day; an earlier daytime threshold used in calculating compensation
key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: financial compensation due for bodily injury
key_terms.الْبَوْلُ: urination; the bodily function whose obstruction is being assessed legally
key_terms.الْمَعِيشَةَ: livelihood or ability to live normally, mentioned as the reason for full compensation
key_terms.نِصْفِ النَّهَارِ: midday; a time marker used to determine the level of compensation

ai.seo_question: What is the diyah for injuring someone so that urination is obstructed for part or all of the day?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling on bodily injury affecting urination and assigns graded diyah according to the duration of the harm. It reflects the concern of Islamic law for physical integrity, human welfare, and compensation for serious impairment that disrupts a person's livelihood.
